repos.title: Exploiting Novel GPT-4 APIs
repos.paper_summary: This paper red-teams three GPT-4 API features—fine-tuning, function calling, and knowledge retrieval—to identify security vulnerabilities. The authors demonstrate that fine-tuning on as few as 15 harmful examples or 100 benign examples removes safety guardrails, increasing the mean harmfulness score from 1.07 to 4.6 out of 5.0 on the AdvBench dataset. They show that a model fine-tuned on 15 anti-public-figure examples mixed with 2,269 benign ones shifts response sentiment from 5% negative to 30% negative. Additionally, they prove that GPT-4 Assistants disclose function call schemas and execute arbitrary unsanitized function calls, including SQL injection attempts. For knowledge retrieval, injecting instructions into uploaded documents causes the model to ignore summarization tasks and instead follow malicious commands, such as executing high-stakes financial transfers. Limitations include the evaluation being restricted to GPT-4 because it is the only frontier model supporting these specific APIs, and the attacks requiring substantial manual prompt engineering rather than full automation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning, function calling and knowledge retrieval in the GPT-4 APIs each introduce new vulnerabilities to the model.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior fine-tuning attacks used weaker models, and the function calling and retrieval features had not been studied.

digest_headlines.heading: Exploiting the OpenAI Fine-Tuning API
digest_headlines.headline: Benign and harmful fine-tuning data remove GPT-4 safeguards, and small poisoned datasets produce targeted misinformation and leaks.

digest_headlines.heading: Red-teaming the OpenAI Assistants API
digest_headlines.headline: The Assistants API leaks function schemas, runs arbitrary calls, and follows injected instructions in retrieved documents.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover only GPT-4, and the attacks still required substantial manual prompt engineering.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The new GPT-4 APIs weaken built-in safeguards, and the authors advise testing new API features even when the underlying model is unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists evaluation prompts, datasets, conspiracy topics, e-mail test names, and attack transcripts for each API feature.

repos.title: LEANN: A Low-Storage Vector Index
repos.paper_summary:
LEANN is a storage-efficient vector index that recomputes embeddings at query time instead of storing them, and prunes the proximity graph while keeping high-degree hub nodes. It builds on HNSW and FAISS. A two-level search uses approximate product-quantization (PQ) distances to select candidates for exact recomputation, and dynamic batching groups recomputations across exploration steps (target batch of 64) to improve GPU use. High-degree preserving pruning keeps the top 2% of nodes by degree at maximum degree M and caps other nodes at M/5.

On a 76 GB text corpus (RPJ-Wiki) with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN uses 4 GB of storage versus 188 GB for HNSW and 20 GB for PQ. End-to-end RAG latency is 23.3 s for LEANN and 21.0 s for HNSW, with 25.5% downstream accuracy for both. Table 2 reports retrieval latency at 90% recall across NQ, GPQA, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA.

Limitations: search latency rises from milliseconds to seconds, which the paper accepts because generation dominates RAG latency. Some baselines (HNSW, IVF) ran on a larger-memory server.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Graph indices for a 76 GB corpus need 188 GB, too large for personal devices, so a smaller index is needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Proximity graph indices need few distance computations, but storage has two parts: vectors and index metadata.

digest_headlines.heading: LEANN Overview
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN keeps a pruned graph and product-quantized codes, recomputing exact embeddings during queries.

digest_headlines.heading: Graph-based Recomputation
digest_headlines.headline: Two-level search and dynamic batching cut recomputation while keeping exact distances for selected candidates.

digest_headlines.heading: Compact Graph Structure
digest_headlines.headline: Preserving edges of the top 2% high-degree nodes shrinks graph metadata while maintaining high retrieval accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Index Building and Update
digest_headlines.headline: Sharded construction and buffered updates limit peak storage during index building and modification.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN matches the accuracy of the standard graph index at 90% recall while storing about 5% of raw data size.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier systems reduce memory via disk layouts, quantization or online embedding but still store embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN keeps the index under 5% of raw data size, up to 50 times smaller than existing methods, with high recall.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers relative neighborhood graph pruning, update algorithms, Mac latency, and ablations on construction, embedding model, caching, and latency breakdown.

repos.title: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
This paper presents an indexing method for guiding large language model generation with regular expressions and context-free grammars, implemented in the Python library `Outlines`. The approach reformulates guided sampling as transitions between finite-state machine (FSM) states. By pre-computing a map from FSM states to valid vocabulary tokens, the algorithm avoids iterating over the entire vocabulary at each step, reducing the average cost of mask construction from $\mathcal{O}(N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$, where $N$ is the vocabulary size.

The method extends to LALR(1) parsers using pushdown automata to enforce syntax for formats like JSON and Python. In benchmarks against the `Guidance` library using GPT-2 on CUDA, the proposed method shows significantly lower latency as sequence length increases, whereas Guidance scales linearly due to repeated full-vocabulary matching. The authors note that while the index requires memory proportional to the number of FSM states, naive indices for augmented Python grammaries remain small, around 50 MB.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Constrained generation over a full vocabulary costs time per token, so the paper proposes a precomputed vocabulary index.

digest_headlines.heading: LLM Sampling and Guided Generation
digest_headlines.headline: Masking invalid tokens each step means checking the whole vocabulary, so guided sampling cost grows with vocabulary size.

digest_headlines.heading: Iterative FSM Processing and Indexing
digest_headlines.headline: Indexing vocabulary strings by FSM state makes mask lookup constant time on average, with memory tied to the number of states.

digest_headlines.heading: Extensions to Iterative Parsing
digest_headlines.headline: Extending the index to parsers pairs finite-state machine states with parser configurations, shown only through a Python-like example.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Naive indices stayed small in tests, and the authors suggest uses in training and lifting masks into the model.

repos.title: Animate Anyone: Consistent and Controllable Image-to-Video Synthesis for Character Animation
repos.paper_summary: Animate Anyone is a diffusion-based framework for pose-controlled image-to-video character animation. It extends Stable Diffusion with three components: ReferenceNet, a parallel UNet that extracts spatial features from the reference image and injects them via spatial attention; a lightweight Pose Guider that adds encoded pose skeletons to the noise latent; and temporal attention layers for inter-frame coherence. Training proceeds in two stages: single-frame denoising, then 24-frame temporal layer training initialized from AnimateDiff weights. On the UBC fashion dataset, it achieves an FVD of 81.6, outperforming DreamPose (279.6) and BDMM (148.3). On TikTok dance data, FVD is 171.9 versus DisCo’s 292.8. The method also improves SSIM to 0.931 on fashion synthesis. Limitations include hand distortions, instability when generating unseen body parts during large motions, and lower inference efficiency compared to non-diffusion baselines due to iterative denoising steps.

repos.title: Eagle and Finch: RWKV with Matrix-Valued States and Dynamic Recurrence
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces Eagle (RWKV-5) and Finch (RWKV-6), RNN-based sequence models that replace vector-valued states with multi-headed matrix-valued states and dynamic recurrence to improve expressivity while maintaining linear-time inference. Eagle adds a SiLU gating mechanism and per-head LayerNorm to the RWKV-4 architecture. Finch extends this by making the decay schedule and token-shift data-dependent using low-rank adaptation matrices. The authors release four Eagle models (0.46B–7.5B parameters) and two Finch models (1.6B, 3.1B) trained on the 1.12 trillion-token RWKV World v2 multilingual dataset. On multilingual benchmarks, Eagle-7B achieves an average accuracy of 58.2%, outperforming LLaMA-2-7B (54.3%) and Mistral-7B (55.5%). Finch-3B reaches 57.1% on multilingual tasks and 67.5% on English tasks. In speed benchmarks, Finch training is 4.2x faster than Flash Attention at 16k sequence length and uses 17% less memory than Mamba. Limitations include weak embedding performance on MTEB and mimicry of ChatGPT conversational styles due to synthetic data in the training corpus.

repos.title: PP-YOLOE: An evolved version of YOLO
repos.paper_summary: PP-YOLOE is a one-stage object detector that modifies PP-YOLOv2 with an anchor-free design, a new backbone and neck, Task Alignment Learning (TAL), and an Efficient Task-aligned Head (ET-head). The backbone uses CSPRepResNet, which builds on RepResBlocks combining residual and dense connections; during inference, these blocks re-parameterize into standard residual blocks. The model scales via width and depth multipliers to produce s, m, l, and x variants. On the COCO test-dev set at 640x640 resolution, PP-YOLOE-l achieves 51.4 mAP and 78.1 FPS on a Tesla V100, outperforming PP-YOLOv2 by 1.9 AP and YOLOX-l by 1.3 AP. With TensorRT and FP16 precision, inference speed reaches 149.2 FPS. Ablation studies show the anchor-free switch costs 0.3 AP, while TAL adds 0.9 AP and ET-head adds 0.5 AP. The paper does not report results for datasets other than MS COCO-2017, and speed comparisons rely on specific hardware configurations without including data preprocessing or non-maximum suppression overhead.

repos.title: FLERT: Document-Level Features for Named Entity Recognition
repos.paper_summary: FLERT evaluates document-level features for named entity recognition by adding 64 subtokens of left and right context to each sentence before passing it through a transformer. The authors compare two architectures: fine-tuning the entire model with a linear classifier, and using frozen XLM-RoBERTa embeddings as input to an LSTM-CRF sequence labeler. Experiments on the CoNLL-03 datasets for English, German, Dutch, and Spanish show that document-level features improve F1-score by an average of 1.15 points over sentence-level baselines. Fine-tuning outperforms the feature-based approach by approximately 2 points across all languages. The best configuration achieves F1-scores of 94.09 on English, 88.34 on German, 95.19 on Dutch, and 90.37 on Spanish when including development data in training. Enforcing document boundaries during context selection further increases performance, indicating that transformers do not automatically respect document limits. A limitation is that the evaluation relies on a single pre-trained multilingual model, XLM-RoBERTa-large, and the results are specific to the CoNLL-03 benchmark.

repos.title: Generalizing to Unseen Domains: A Survey on Domain Generalization
repos.paper_summary:
This paper presents the first comprehensive survey of domain generalization (DG), a setting where models trained on one or more source domains must generalize to an unseen target domain. The authors categorize DG algorithms into three classes: data manipulation, representation learning, and learning strategy. Data manipulation methods include augmentation via randomization or adversarial generation, and data synthesis using GANs or Mixup. Representation learning focuses on domain-invariant features through kernel methods, adversarial training, invariant risk minimization, and feature disentanglement. Learning strategy approaches utilize ensemble learning, meta-learning, gradient operations, and distributionally robust optimization.

The survey reviews theoretical bounds for DG, including average risk estimation error and generalization risk under covariate shift assumptions. It also introduces `DeepDG`, an open-source codebase for fair evaluation across public datasets. Limitations noted include the lack of theoretical guarantees for unbounded risk in data manipulation methods and the observation that adversarial training yields less significant improvements in DG compared to domain adaptation.

repos.title: Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks
repos.paper_summary: The paper presents an updated open-source benchmarking framework for graph neural networks, adding the AQSOL molecular dataset to a collection of 12 medium-scale datasets. The framework enforces fair model comparison by fixing parameter budgets at 100k and 500k, ensuring performance differences reflect architectural design rather than capacity. It includes modular code for data pipelines, GNN layers, and training protocols built on PyTorch and DGL. As a proof of concept, the authors demonstrate how the benchmark identifies the utility of Laplacian eigenvectors as positional encodings, which improve message-passing GCNs on synthetic datasets like CSL and CYCLES where standard models fail due to node anonymity. The primary limitation is that the medium-scale datasets are selected for rapid prototyping within 12-hour experimental runs, meaning results may not directly extrapolate to large-scale industrial graphs requiring extensive GPU resources.

repos.title: Reproducible scaling laws for contrastive language-image learning
repos.paper_summary:
This paper establishes reproducible power-law scaling relationships for contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP) using the public LAION dataset and open-source OpenCLIP code. The authors trained models ranging from ViT-B/32 to ViT-g/14 on up to 2.3 billion image-text pairs, varying model size, data scale, and samples seen. They evaluate performance on zero-shot classification, retrieval, linear probing, and fine-tuning.

The study finds that downstream accuracy follows a power law with respect to total compute. For zero-shot ImageNet classification, the scaling coefficient is $-0.11$ for LAION-trained models versus $-0.16$ for OpenAI’s WIT-400M-trained models. Conversely, for MS-COCO retrieval, LAION models show stronger scaling ($-0.08$) than OpenAI models ($-0.05$). This indicates that training distribution significantly influences task-specific scaling behavior. Using these laws, the authors predict that a ViT-G/14 model trained on 68 billion samples would achieve 81.9% zero-shot top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. Limitations include low sampling density in the scale space due to compute constraints and the inability to fully tune hyperparameters at larger scales.
